## Simple explanation

A feature store helps teams define, manage, and serve model features
consistently. It can provide shared feature definitions for training and
for predictions in production.

## Technical explanation

Feature stores commonly support offline storage for historical training
data and online storage for low-latency serving. They may manage feature
transformations, metadata, lineage, freshness, and point-in-time retrieval.
Capabilities and architectures vary between products.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Feature stores can reduce duplicated feature logic and help avoid
training-serving skew. They introduce infrastructure and governance
requirements, so they are most useful when shared features and operational
needs justify the added system.

## How it works

Feature definitions are registered and computed from source data. The
system stores historical values for training and may publish recent
values to an online store for inference. Point-in-time joins help ensure
training examples use only values available at the prediction time.

## Practical example

A fraud model can use a customer's transaction count over the previous
24 hours. An offline store provides historical values for training,
while an online store serves the current count to production predictions.

## Common misconceptions

- A feature store does not guarantee that feature definitions are
  correct or free from leakage.
- It is not necessarily required for a small project or a single model.
- Offline and online feature values can differ unless transformations
  and freshness are managed carefully.
